How to Find and Use eBay Sold Comps

Research comparable eBay sales, handle Best Offers and shipping differences, and turn sold-price evidence into a realistic sourcing estimate.

Sold comps are comparable items that have sold. They help answer a question that comes before a profit calculation: what selling price can you reasonably plan around? A high asking price alone is not evidence that a buyer will pay it.

1. Find sold items, then check the match

Start with the exact brand and model, adding size, edition, or a part number when relevant. In eBay Advanced Search, select Sold items. The form also offers Completed items; use the sold filter when gathering sale-price evidence rather than treating every ended listing as a sale.

Open individual results and check the description and photos. A matching title can hide a missing accessory, an untested unit, or a different version. Keep a short record for each usable comp:

  • Listing link, date checked, and sale date
  • Exact model, size, condition, and included accessories
  • Single item or bundle, and quantity included
  • Item price, buyer-paid shipping, and currency
  • Sale format and whether the actual accepted price is known

2. Resolve Best Offers and narrow the search

If the accepted offer amount is unclear, do not record the original asking price as the sale price. eBay says Product Research includes actual sold prices, including accepted Best Offers. It also supports condition, location, and listing-format filters. Check availability in your eBay account; MarginFlips does not retrieve listings or require you to sign in here.

Use a consistent date range and marketplace. Separate auctions from fixed-price sales when they represent different selling plans. Exclude parts-only items, unrelated models, and bundles you cannot compare fairly. If a result is unusually high or low, investigate its condition and contents before deciding whether it belongs in your sample.

3. Compare shipping on the same basis

Comparable buyer total before tax = item price + buyer-paid shipping

This total helps compare a free-shipping listing with one charging postage separately. It is not seller profit: you still need your own postage, fees, purchase cost, and preparation costs. Keep currencies consistent and record shipping separately so it is not counted twice.

A worked example: a used game controller

Illustrative numbers only, not observed eBay sales or a market-price claim. Suppose you find three equally comparable, tested controllers in the same currency and condition:

  • Comp A: $32 item price + $6 buyer-paid shipping = $38 before tax.
  • Comp B: $40 item price + $0 shipping = $40 before tax.
  • Comp C: $36 item price + $5 buyer-paid shipping = $41 before tax.

The middle buyer total is $40. That is a reference point, not a guaranteed sale price. A $15 parts-only controller and a $65 two-controller bundle would not belong in this same comparison. With only these three examples, confidence is limited; look for more close matches rather than inventing an adjustment percentage.

If you plan to offer free shipping, you could test $38 as a cautious scenario and $40 as a middle scenario in the maximum buy price calculator. Enter your own seller-paid shipping and verified fee assumptions. For this example, use a $6 postage estimate, a hypothetical 13% fee, a $0.30 fixed fee, and a $12 target profit, with no other costs:

At $38: $38 − $4.94 fees − $0.30 − $6 − $12 = $14.76 maximum buy price
At $40: $40 − $5.20 fees − $0.30 − $6 − $12 = $16.50 maximum buy price

These fee and postage inputs are examples, not current eBay rates. Add packaging and preparation costs to your non-item costs before sourcing. If your deal only works at the highest comp, revisit the purchase price or pass. Use the profit calculator to check the resulting scenario.

4. Know when the evidence is too weak

  • No close sold matches: broaden one search detail at a time and record the differences. No results do not establish a zero value or prove there is no demand.
  • One unusually high sale: do not treat it as a reliable price range. Check for rare variants or extras you do not have.
  • Old or seasonal sales: compare their timing with when you intend to sell. Historical prices may not describe today's competition.
  • Unclear condition or accepted price: mark the result as uncertain rather than filling the gap with a guess.
  • Plenty of active listings: asking prices show competition, not completed transactions or a promise of how quickly your item will sell.

5. Save the evidence alongside the decision

Keep your comp links, exclusions, price range, and date checked in your own research notes. Record the chosen selling-price assumption and purchase decision in a sourcing log, then compare it with the eventual sale. The Reseller Profit Tool brings a Sourcing Log, Sales Log, and pricing calculations into one workbook; your comp research supplies the assumptions rather than being automatically imported.

Before buying, finish the reseller sourcing checklist for condition, restrictions, and shipping practicality. Reliable comps improve an estimate; they cannot guarantee demand or profit.

Sources checked September 11, 2026: eBay Advanced Search and eBay Product Research, linked above. Interface labels and availability can change.

Keep the estimate honest.
